title: How would you design a social feed / timeline at scale (e.g. Instagram/Twitter) — fanout-on-write (push a fully denormalized post entry into each follower's precomputed timeline so reads are an O(1) list lookup) vs fanout-on-read (pull + merge at read time), and why do you use a HYBRID (fanout-on-write for normal users, fanout-on-read for celebrities with millions of followers to avoid massive write amplification)?
shortTitle: How would you design a social feed / timeline at scale
topicTitle: How would you design a social feed / timeline at scale (e.g. Instagram/Twitter)

s1_definition.profdef: A social feed at scale precomputes or assembles each user's timeline of posts from the people they follow. There are two strategies. Fanout-on-write pushes each new post into every follower's precomputed timeline at post time, so reading a feed is a cheap, near-constant-time list lookup, at the cost of write amplification proportional to the follower count. Fanout-on-read stores posts once and assembles the feed by pulling and merging the followees' recent posts at read time, which keeps writes cheap but makes reads expensive and fan-in heavy. Because neither extreme works for everyone, large systems use a hybrid: fanout-on-write for normal users whose follower counts are modest, and fanout-on-read for celebrities with millions of followers, where writing to millions of timelines per post would be prohibitive, so their posts are merged in at read time instead.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India sending account-activity notices. Fanout-on-write is like the moment something happens, immediately stuffing a copy of the notice into every interested customer's personal mailbox, so when a customer opens their mailbox it is already full and instant to read, but if one event interests a million customers you must stuff a million mailboxes. Fanout-on-read is like keeping one master noticeboard and, whenever a customer asks, running around gathering the relevant notices and sorting them, which is cheap to post but slow to read. The hybrid is the sensible branch policy: for ordinary notices with a few interested people, pre-stuff the mailboxes; for a notice that interests millions, do not stuff a million mailboxes, instead fetch that one on demand and blend it into what the customer sees.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fanout-on-write precomputes each follower's timeline for O(1) reads but amplifies writes by follower count, fanout-on-read keeps writes cheap but makes reads expensive, and the hybrid uses fanout-on-write for normal users and fanout-on-read for celebrities to avoid writing to millions of timelines per post.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A social feed at scale precomputes or assembles each user's timeline of posts from the people they follow. There are two strategies. Fanout-on-write pushes each new post into every follower's precomputed timeline at post time, so reading a feed is a cheap, near-constant-time list lookup, at the cost of write amplification proportional to the follower count. Fanout-on-read stores posts once and assembles the feed by pulling and merging the followees' recent posts at read time, which keeps writes cheap but makes reads expensive and fan-in heavy. Because neither extreme works for everyone, large systems use a hybrid: fanout-on-write for normal users whose follower counts are modest, and fanout-on-read for celebrities with millions of followers, where writing to millions of timelines per post would be prohibitive, so their posts are merged in at read time instead.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India sending account-activity notices. Fanout-on-write is like the moment something happens, immediately stuffing a copy of the notice into every interested customer's personal mailbox, so when a customer opens their mailbox it is already full and instant to read, but if one event interests a million customers you must stuff a million mailboxes. Fanout-on-read is like keeping one master noticeboard and, whenever a customer asks, running around gathering the relevant notices and sorting them, which is cheap to post but slow to read. The hybrid is the sensible branch policy: for ordinary notices with a few interested people, pre-stuff the mailboxes; for a notice that interests millions, do not stuff a million mailboxes, instead fetch that one on demand and blend it into what the customer sees.

**One line to remember:** Fanout-on-write precomputes each follower's timeline for O(1) reads but amplifies writes by follower count, fanout-on-read keeps writes cheap but makes reads expensive, and the hybrid uses fanout-on-write for normal users and fanout-on-read for celebrities to avoid writing to millions of timelines per post.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the fundamental tension: a feed read is extremely frequent and must be fast, while posting is comparatively rare, but a single post can affect a huge number of followers. You are trading where you pay the cost, at write time or at read time, and the follower-count distribution, which is wildly skewed, is what forces a hybrid.

Fanout-on-write, also called push, does the work when a post is created. At post time you look up the author's followers and push a reference to the new post, often a fully denormalized entry with the fields needed to render it, into each follower's precomputed timeline, typically a per-user list in a fast store like Redis or a wide-column store. Reading a feed is then a simple read of that precomputed list, which is near constant time and very fast, exactly what you want for the read-heavy feed. The cost is write amplification: one post by someone with N followers triggers N writes. For normal users with hundreds or a few thousand followers this is perfectly fine and the fast reads are well worth it. The denormalized entry avoids a join at read time, trading storage for read speed.

Fanout-on-read, also called pull, does the work when the feed is requested. You store each post once in the author's own posts collection and compute nothing at write time. When a user opens their feed, you fetch the recent posts of everyone they follow and merge them, usually by time, into a single ordered timeline. Writes are now trivial, a single insert per post regardless of followers, but reads are expensive: a user following hundreds of accounts triggers a large fan-in query and a merge on every feed load, which is slow and costly at scale. Pull is attractive for authors with enormous follower counts because it avoids the write explosion, and for inactive users whose timelines would be computed but rarely read.

Now the decisive problem that makes pure strategies fail: the follower distribution is extremely skewed. Most users have few followers, but a small number of celebrities have millions. Pure fanout-on-write collapses on celebrities, because a single celebrity post would trigger millions of timeline writes, a thundering write storm that is slow, expensive, and spiky, and it wastes effort writing into the timelines of followers who may never open the app. Pure fanout-on-read collapses on normal reads, because every feed load for every user becomes an expensive multi-account merge, losing the fast-read benefit for the common case. So neither extreme is acceptable across the whole population.

The hybrid resolves this by choosing the strategy per author based on follower count. For normal users, you use fanout-on-write: their posts are pushed into followers' precomputed timelines, giving fast reads for the vast majority of content. For celebrities above some follower threshold, you use fanout-on-read: their posts are not fanned out to millions of timelines; instead each follower's feed is assembled by taking their precomputed timeline from normal followees and merging in the celebrity's recent posts pulled at read time. A follower's feed load therefore reads their small precomputed list plus a handful of pulls for the few celebrities they follow, which is both fast and avoids the write storm. This captures the best of both: cheap, fast reads for ordinary content, and no catastrophic write amplification for mega-accounts.

Several supporting details make this production-grade. You cache celebrity recent posts aggressively, since they are pulled by many followers, so the read-time merge is cheap. You cap the size of precomputed timelines, keeping only the most recent entries, because feeds are rarely scrolled far back, which bounds storage. You handle the write fanout asynchronously through a queue so posting returns immediately and the fanout happens in the background, smoothing spikes. You rank and merge by time or by a relevance score, and you deduplicate. You also handle edge cases like a user crossing the celebrity threshold, at which point you switch their strategy, and new follows, where you may backfill a bit of the followee's recent history into the new follower's timeline.

Senior nuances worth stating: store denormalized timeline entries so reads need no joins, but keep them small and reference the canonical post for full content and edits; make fanout asynchronous and idempotent so retries do not duplicate timeline entries; choose the celebrity threshold from the actual follower distribution and revisit it, since it directly trades write cost against read cost; cache celebrity posts and hot timelines; cap and page timelines to bound storage and latency; and treat deletes and privacy changes carefully, since a deleted or now-private post must not appear in precomputed timelines, which argues for storing references and resolving visibility at read time. The whole design is an exercise in paying the cost where it is cheapest for each class of user, which is exactly why the hybrid exists.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs an internal investor-updates feed where analysts and companies post market updates and customers like Rajesh and Priya follow the ones they care about, and the feed must open instantly. This is exactly the read-heavy feed problem, solved by fanout-on-write precomputing each follower's timeline for near-constant-time reads.

Problem 2 — A hugely popular market index account has millions of followers, and pushing each of its posts into millions of timelines would cause a write storm. This is exactly the write-amplification problem, solved by treating that account as a celebrity and using fanout-on-read for its posts.

Problem 3 — A customer's feed must combine both: the precomputed posts from the normal analysts they follow and the latest from the celebrity index account. This is exactly the hybrid assembly, solved by reading the precomputed timeline and merging in the celebrity's cached recent posts at read time.

Our mini-project builds a hybrid feed core. The code fans out normal authors' posts on write into per-follower timelines, treats high-follower authors as celebrities whose posts are pulled and merged at read time, and assembles a customer's feed by combining the two. The demo posts normal updates and a celebrity update, then builds Rajesh's feed.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh follows two normal analysts and one celebrity index account with five million followers; two analysts post, the celebrity posts, then Rajesh opens his feed.

Step 1: Analyst A posts a banking-sector update. Because analyst A has only five hundred followers, the system uses fanout-on-write and pushes the post into each of those five hundred followers' precomputed timelines, including Rajesh's. The write cost is five hundred small writes, which is cheap.

Step 2: Analyst B posts a rate-decision update. Analyst B has two thousand followers, still well under the celebrity threshold, so fanout-on-write pushes the post into two thousand timelines, again including Rajesh's. His precomputed timeline now holds both analyst posts, newest first.

Step 3: The celebrity index account posts that the index hit an all-time high. Because it has five million followers, above the celebrity threshold, the system does not fan this out. Writing into five million timelines would be a write storm, so instead the post is stored once in the celebrity's recent-posts store for pull at read time. The write cost is a single insert regardless of five million followers.

Step 4: Rajesh opens his feed. The feed service first reads his precomputed timeline, which already contains the two analyst posts, in near-constant time with no joins or merges. This is the fast common-case read that fanout-on-write provides.

Step 5: The feed service then looks at whom Rajesh follows, finds the one celebrity index account, and pulls that account's cached recent posts, merging in the all-time-high post. Only a handful of pulls are needed because a user follows few celebrities, so the read-time merge is small and cheap.

Step 6: The combined feed, the two precomputed analyst posts plus the pulled celebrity post, is returned to Rajesh. In production these would be merged by timestamp or relevance, deduplicated, and paginated, but the key point is that Rajesh got a fast feed while the system never wrote to five million timelines for one celebrity post.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:12:40 INFO    fanout-on-WRITE: pushed 'Banking sector up 2%' into 1 timelines
2026-10-24 15:12:40 INFO    fanout-on-WRITE: pushed 'Rate decision at 2pm' into 1 timelines
2026-10-24 15:12:40 INFO    fanout-on-READ: stored celebrity post 'Nifty hits all-time high' (NOT fanned out)
2026-10-24 15:12:40 INFO    Rajesh feed = [Rate decision at 2pm, Banking sector up 2%, Nifty hits all-time high]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── POST (strategy chosen PER AUTHOR by follower count) ──
  ANALYST-A posts (500 followers < 1M)
    │ fanout-on-WRITE (async queue)
    ▼
  push into each follower's precomputed timeline  [write amplification = #followers]
    Rajesh.timeline = [A-post]

  INDEX-NIFTY posts (5,000,000 followers ≥ 1M = CELEBRITY)
    │ fanout-on-READ
    ▼
  store ONCE in celebrity recent-posts (cached)   [write = 1, NO 5M-timeline storm]

  ── READ (feed open) ──
  Rajesh opens feed
    │
    ├─ read precomputed timeline  ──────────▶ [B-post, A-post]   O(1), no joins
    │
    └─ for each CELEBRITY followed (few):
         pull recent cached posts ──merge──▶ + [Nifty all-time high]
    │
    ▼
  merge by time/score + dedupe + paginate
  Rajesh feed = [B-post, A-post, Nifty all-time high]

  WHY HYBRID:
   pure push  → celebrity post = millions of writes (storm) ✗
   pure pull  → every feed open = big multi-account merge (slow) ✗
   hybrid     → fast reads for normal + no storm for celebrities ✓
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A social feed at scale is a trade-off about where you pay the cost, at write time or at read time, and the skewed follower distribution is what forces the answer. Fanout-on-write pushes each new post into every follower's precomputed timeline at post time, so reading a feed is a near-constant-time list lookup, which is exactly what the read-heavy feed needs, but one post by someone with N followers triggers N writes. Fanout-on-read stores each post once and assembles the feed by pulling and merging the followees' recent posts at read time, so writes are trivial but every feed load becomes an expensive multi-account merge.

Neither pure strategy works across the whole population because of the distribution. Most users have few followers, but a small number of celebrities have millions. Pure fanout-on-write collapses on a celebrity, because one post would trigger millions of timeline writes, a slow, expensive, spiky write storm that also wastes effort on followers who never open the app. Pure fanout-on-read collapses on normal reads, because every feed load becomes a big fan-in merge and you lose the fast-read benefit for the common case.

So I use a hybrid that chooses the strategy per author by follower count. Normal users get fanout-on-write, so their posts are precomputed into followers' timelines and the vast majority of content reads instantly. Celebrities above a follower threshold get fanout-on-read, so their posts are stored once and merged into each follower's feed at read time instead of being written to millions of timelines. A follower's feed load then reads their small precomputed timeline plus a handful of pulls for the few celebrities they follow, which is both fast and free of the write storm. I support this with aggressive caching of celebrity posts since many followers pull the same ones, capping timelines to recent entries to bound storage, doing the write fanout asynchronously through a queue so posting returns immediately, and merging by time or relevance with deduplication.

On my project at National Bank of India we built an investor-updates feed exactly this way. Analysts with modest followings were fanned out on write so customers like Rajesh and Priya opened their feeds instantly, while a market-index account with millions of followers was treated as a celebrity and pulled at read time, so one index update did not trigger millions of timeline writes. Rajesh's feed was assembled by reading his precomputed timeline of analyst posts and merging in the cached recent posts of the one celebrity account he followed. The design lesson I stress is that the hybrid exists specifically to pay the cost where it is cheapest for each class of user, and the celebrity threshold is the knob that trades write cost against read cost, so I set it from the real follower distribution and revisit it.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that fanout-on-write precomputes timelines for fast O(1) reads but amplifies writes by follower count, fanout-on-read keeps writes cheap but makes reads a costly merge, and the hybrid uses fanout-on-write for normal users and fanout-on-read for celebrities so that ordinary content reads instantly while a mega-account's post never triggers a write to millions of timelines.
